You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 6 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

what this means:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out}$ between 4.5V and 5.5V.
    *   Ripple: $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$.
    *   Startup: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    *   Settled: $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   Note: $V_{oc}$ (3.8V) is lower than the target $V_{out}$ (4.5V-5.5V), so we *must* have some form of voltage boost (like SSHI or a charge pump/doubler).

    *   P-SSHI (Topology `6e6749432f4c`) is the strongest design (Score 40.40).
    *   It passes S2 and S6.
    *   It fails:
        *   S1, S3, S5: $V_{max} > 5.5\text{V}$ (overvoltage).
        *   S4: $V_{min} < 4.5\text{V}$ (underpower) and $t_{up}$ failure.
        *   S3, S5: $\Delta V$ too high (long settling time).

    *   The overvoltage on S1, S3, S5 suggests we need a way to clamp $V_{out}$ at 5.5V.
    *   The underpower on S4 suggests we need to maximize efficiency or a more robust boost.
    *   The long settling time suggests the storage capacitor $C_{out}$ might be too large or the power delivered too close to the load power.
    *   Looking at the P-SSHI topology:
        ```
        D1 D pzp out DSCH
        D2 D pzn out DSCH
        D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
        D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
        L1 L pzp n1 0.01
        S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
        G1 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0.00271 edges=both
        C1 C out 0 6.13e-07
        ```
        This is a standard SSHI circuit where $L_1$ and $S_1$ perform the inversion of $C_p$. The diodes $D_1-D_4$ form a full-bridge rectifier.

    *   To fix $V_{max} > 5.5\text{V}$, we need a clamp. A Zener diode (DZ33) is 3.3V, which is too low. We need a 5.5V clamp. Since we don't have a 5.5V Zener, we can use a string of Zeners or another method. However, the available Zener is `DZ33` (3.3V).
    *   Wait, I can't use a 5.5V Zener. How to clamp $V_{out}$ to 5.5V? Maybe a simple shunt regulator or a different topology?
    *   Let's rethink the clamping. If $V_{out}$ exceeds 5.5V, we need to bleed off current. A resistor is too inefficient.
    *   Could we use a Zener-based clamp? $DZ33$ is 3.3V. If I put two in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$. Too high.
    *   What about the "underpower" on S4? S4 is weak excitation ($I_p = 40\text{uA}$, $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$). The current is low, but the load is also very light.

    *   P-SSHI provides a boost. To prevent $V_{out}$ from going too high, we can use a Zener clamp *if* the Zener voltage was correct.
    *   Alternatively, we can use a "bleeder" resistor, but the results for `P-SSHI-Bleed` were poor (underpower).
    *   The problem with P-SSHI was mostly $V_{max}$ and S4's $V_{min}$.
    *   Let's consider the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or a variation.
    *   Actually, the simplest fix for overvoltage in these circuits is often a shunt or a voltage-limiting stage. But the constraints on components are tight.

    *   Let's try adding a Zener clamp to P-SSHI. But `DZ33` is 3.3V. That would clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V, which is below the 4.5V minimum.
    *   Wait, I can use the `DZ33` in a different way? No, it's a Zener.
    *   What if I use a different boost topology? Like a Dickson charge pump or a switched-capacitor converter?
    *   The "Doubler-SSHI" failed.
    *   Let's try a modified P-SSHI with a way to limit the output. If I can't clamp it, maybe I can adjust the tuning (though I don't control the tuner, I control the topology).
    *   The tuner failed to keep $V_{out} \le 5.5\text{V}$ on S1, S3, S5. This means the power extracted is *too* high for the load.
    *   If I add a small parallel resistor to the load, it might lower $V_{out}$ on S3 but make S4 worse.

    *   S4: $I_p = 40\text{uA}$, $f=100\text{Hz}$, $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$. $P_{load} = 4.5^2 / 4.7\text{M} \approx 4.3\text{uW}$.
    *   P-SSHI on S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77\text{V}$. This is close to 4.5V but not quite there.
    *   This means the P-SSHI is nearly efficient enough, but not quite.
    *   Maybe a more efficient SSHI? The current P-SSHI uses a full bridge. A half-bridge (with a floating capacitor) is often more efficient.

    *   Wait, the "P-SSHI" provided is:
        $D_1$ (pzp $\to$ out), $D_2$ (pzn $\to$ out), $D_3$ (0 $\to$ pzp), $D_4$ (0 $\to$ pzn).
        This is a full bridge.
        $L_1$ (pzp $\to$ n1), $S_1$ (n1 $\to$ pzn).
        This is the SSHI part.
        When $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ and $C_p$ exchange energy.
        This is the "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI).

    *   To improve S4 (underpower) and S3 (overvoltage), we need a way to regulate.
    *   What if we use a "Symmetric-SSHI" or "SECE"?
    *   Let's try a SECE-like structure. SECE typically uses a switch and an inductor to transfer the charge of $C_p$ to the output at the peaks.

    *   SECE Topology:
        - Inductor $L$ in series with a switch $S$ and a diode $D$ to the output.
        - This usually requires a more complex switch arrangement.

    *   Let's try an "Inductive-Boost" bridge:
        The P-SSHI is already doing this. Let's try to make it more efficient.
        The full bridge has two diode drops. A half-bridge has one.
        Half-bridge SSHI:
        $C_{fly}$ between pzn and some node `mid`.
        $D_1$ from `mid` to `out`.
        $D_2$ from `pzn` to `mid` (through something?). No.

    *   Actually, let's try a different approach for the overvoltage. If we can't use a Zener, can we use a "crowbar" or a shunt? We have no active components other than SYNC.
    *   What if we use a "voltage doubler" combined with the SSHI? No, that's likely to increase overvoltage.

    *   Let's try to improve the P-SSHI by changing the diode configuration to reduce losses.
        The current P-SSHI:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        This is a standard bridge.

    *   What if we use a different inversion method?
        P-SSHI with a different $L-S$ placement?
        Current: $L_1$ (pzp-n1), $S_1$ (n1-pzn).
        When $S_1$ closes, the loop is $pzp \to L_1 \to n1 \to S_1 \to pzn \to C_p \to pzp$.
        This is correct.

    *   Let's look at the failures again.
        S3: $V_{max} = 12.2\text{V}$. $R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$.
        S4: $V_{avg} = 3.77\text{V}$. $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$.
        S1: $V_{max} = 5.58\text{V}$. $R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$.
        S5: $V_{max} = 6.1\text{V}$. $R_L = 3.3\text{M}\Omega$.

        The overvoltage is very severe when $R_L$ is large (S3). The underpower is on S4.
        This is a wide range of $R_L$ (2.2M to 10M) and $I_p$ (40uA to 120uA).
        A simple SSHI is an open-loop converter. The output voltage depends on $P_{in}/P_{load}$.
        To fix this, we need a way to limit $V_{out}$ without wasting too much power on S4.

    *   Is there a way to use the `DZ33` Zener to regulate?
        If we use a Zener-based regulator, we could clamp the output. But `DZ33` is 3.3V.
        Could we use a Zener in a "feedback" loop? No, we have no OpAmps.
        What if we use the Zener to trigger the SYNC? No, the SYNC is ideal and tracks the piezo.

    *   Let's consider a "Charge-Pump" based approach.
        A Dickson charge pump or a Greinacher circuit.
        A Greinacher circuit:
        $C_1$ (pzp $\to$ n1)
        $D_1$ (n1 $\to$ out)
        $D_2$ (pzn $\to$ n1)
        $C_2$ (out $\to$ 0)
        This doubles the voltage. With $V_{oc} = 3.8\text{V}$, $2 \times 3.8 = 7.6\text{V}$.
        This might be enough for S4, and we could use a Zener to clamp? No, still 3.3V.

    *   Wait, if I use the `DZ33` to clamp the *input* of the doubler? No.
    *   What if I use the `DZ33` in series?
        A diode $D$ and a Zener $DZ$ in series: $V_{drop} = 0.25 + 3.3 = 3.55\text{V}$.
        If I put this in the output path? No.

    *   Let's try to optimize the P-SSHI for the "worst case" S4 and hope the tuner can handle the others. But the tuner already tried 48 evaluations.
        The problem is the $V_{max}$ on S3.
        S3: $I_p = 120\text{uA}$, $R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$.
        The extracted power is much higher than the load power.
        $P_{extracted} \approx V_{out} \cdot I_{out} = 12\text{V} \cdot (12\text{V}/10\text{M}\Omega) \approx 14.4\text{uW}$.
        $P_{load} = 4.5^2 / 10\text{M} \approx 2\text{uW}$.
        So it's delivering $\sim 7$ times the needed power.

        How to limit $V_{out}$?
        If we add a shunt resistor $R_{shunt}$, we need $V_{out}/R_{shunt} \approx P_{extracted} - P_{load}$.
        For S3: $12\text{V}/R_{shunt} \approx 12\text{uW} \implies R_{shunt} \approx 1\text{M}\Omega$.
        But if we add $1\text{M}\Omega$ shunt, then on S4:
        $P_{load\_total} = 4.5^2 / 4.7\text{M} + 4.5^2 / 1\text{M} \approx 4.3\text{uW} + 20\text{uW} = 24.3\text{uW}$.
        On S4, the P-SSHI delivered $3.77\text{V}$, meaning it delivers $3.77^2 / 4.7\text{M} \approx 3\text{uW}$.
        Adding a shunt will just drop the voltage further. So a shunt resistor won't work.

    *   We need a more efficient converter to lift S4 and a way to clamp S3.
        Wait, the `DZ33` is a Zener. If I put it in *series* with the load?
        The load is $R_L$ from `out` to `0`.
        If I put `out` $\to$ `DZ33` $\to$ $R_L \to 0$?
        Then the voltage across $R_L$ would be $V_{out} - 3.3\text{V}$.
        To get 4.5V across $R_L$, we need $V_{out} = 7.8\text{V}$.
        But the requirement is $V_{out}$ (the node "out") must be 4.5V-5.5V.
        So the load is connected to `out`.

    *   Let's try the "Half-Bridge SSHI" to see if we can get more power for S4.
        A half-bridge SSHI:
        $C_{fly}$ between `pzn` and `n1`.
        $D_1$ from `n1` to `out`.
        $L_1$ and $S_1$ for inversion.
